summary: Task 5 implements registration, email verification, and resend cleanly with strong cross-file consistency, good DTO/validation design, and well-explained spec deviations. The blocker is one reactive-correctness regression: `AuthService.register()` calls `passwordEncoder.encode()` (BCrypt cost 12, ~250ms blocking) directly inside a `.map()` on the Netty event loop. The login path uses the correct `Mono.fromCallable(...).subscribeOn(boundedElastic())` pattern; registration was not migrated to it.

criticalIssues.issue: BCrypt password encoding (`passwordEncoder.encode(...)` at line 235 inside `applyRegistration`) is invoked synchronously from `.map(slot -> applyRegistration(...))` (line 124-125). With BCrypt cost 12 (Decision 3), this is a ~250ms CPU-bound blocking call running on the Reactor Netty event loop, which serves all HTTP requests. Under modest concurrent registration load this will stall every other in-flight reactive request on the same event loop thread. The login flow correctly wraps `passwordEncoder.matches(...)` in `Mono.fromCallable(...).subscribeOn(Schedulers.boundedElastic())` (lines 295-296, 305-306) — registration must follow the same pattern.
criticalIssues.impact: Event-loop starvation under load: a single registration burst can degrade latency for all concurrent requests (login, verify-email, /me, future endpoints). Direct violation of WebFlux non-blocking I/O constraint that is the central architectural rationale of this project (architecture.md row 1: 'Reactive, non-blocking I/O — critical for high-throughput Telegram webhook processing').
criticalIssues.recommendation: Refactor `applyRegistration` so the BCrypt call is isolated and offloaded. Minimal change: move `passwordEncoder.encode(req.getPassword())` into its own `Mono.fromCallable(() -> passwordEncoder.encode(req.getPassword())).subscribeOn(Schedulers.boundedElastic())` step in `register()`, then map its result into the user entity. Same scheduler the login path already uses. Also consider offloading `tokenService.generateRawToken()` (SecureRandom can block on entropy depletion in rare cases) but BCrypt is the urgent fix.

suggestions.suggestion: `register(RegisterRequest, ServerWebExchange exchange)` accepts `exchange` but never reads it (no IP/UA capture, no event logging from register). Either drop the parameter (and update controller signature) or add a `registration_started`/`registration_succeeded` event log for parity with login. Currently it is dead arg that suggests behaviour that is not there.
suggestions.benefit: Removes misleading API surface; matches the principle of least surprise (other auth methods that take `exchange` actually use it for IP and UA extraction).

suggestions.suggestion: `resendVerification()` does not log any audit event on success (new token issued) or on rate-limit trip. Login logs `login_failed` with `reason=brute_force` for its rate-limit trip; resend should similarly log a `resend_throttled` (or reuse `login_failed` schema with a new reason) so SOC tooling can detect enumeration attempts that probe the resend endpoint. Acceptance criteria do not require it, but it matches the audit-logging discipline established in Task 4.
suggestions.benefit: Closes an audit-trail gap that an attacker can use to probe the resend endpoint without leaving a trace beyond Redis TTL.

suggestions.suggestion: `canonicalize(null)` returns empty string which then becomes the Redis key `resend:rate:` and the lookup key for `findByEmail("")`. Bean Validation `@NotBlank @Email` on the DTO blocks the request before it reaches the service, so this is defensive only — but a `null`-input branch in service code that ends up writing an empty-string Redis key is a latent footgun. Consider throwing `AppException.badRequest(...)` on null/blank instead of silently coercing.
suggestions.benefit: Fail-loud over fail-quiet; shrinks the surface where a future caller bypassing the controller layer can poison Redis.

suggestions.suggestion: Both `register()` (line 132) and `resendVerification()` (line 198-199) log `saved.getEmail()` at WARN on email dispatch failure. Email addresses are PII (GDPR Article 4). This pattern is already established in `EmailService` (line 93) and Task 4 events, so it is consistent with the codebase — but the global stance on logging email PII should be documented in `patterns.md` so reviewers do not flag this repeatedly.
suggestions.benefit: Establishes a documented project-wide stance on PII in logs; prevents future inconsistency.

suggestions.suggestion: `verifyEmail` query parameter is not validated against length/charset. A pathological 1MB token in the query string would still reach `tokenService.hashToken(...)` and SHA-256 it. Add `@Size(max=128)` (or a hard length check at the service entry) — base64url-of-32-bytes is always 43 chars, so anything beyond ~64 chars is definitionally invalid.
suggestions.benefit: Cheap DoS hardening; the existing `if (rawToken.isBlank())` check in the service can be extended to also reject excessively long inputs.

suggestions.suggestion: `register_invalidPassword_noDigit_400` asserts `$.message` contains the substring `"password"`. The actual message comes from Bean Validation default formatting (`GlobalErrorHandler` for `BindException` / `WebExchangeBindException`) and is locale-sensitive. If the JVM default locale flips on the CI runner, this assertion can break. Consider asserting on a stable structural field (e.g. an `errors` list with the field name) instead of the human-readable string.
suggestions.benefit: Removes locale fragility from the IT suite.

suggestions.suggestion: Static container start in a `static {}` block with no shutdown hook means containers persist for the JVM lifetime — Testcontainers' Ryuk handles cleanup, but if Ryuk is disabled (CI policy at some orgs), containers leak. Consider switching to the singleton-pattern with `@SuppressWarnings("resource")` justified by Ryuk reliance, and adding a JVM shutdown hook that calls `.stop()` for resilience.
suggestions.benefit: Defensive cleanup if Ryuk is ever disabled in CI.

suggestions.suggestion: Magic literal `1L` in `count != null && count == 1L` (line 333). Pre-existing from Task 4, but the Task 5 diff did not extract a constant. Consider `private static final long FIRST_INCREMENT = 1L;` for readability.
suggestions.benefit: Self-documenting code; aligns with the named-constants discipline applied elsewhere in this file (`EMAIL_THRESHOLD`, `BRUTE_TTL`, etc.).
